name: Deliverables & templates — consistent, templated documents
tagline: Stop accepting a wall of chat text when you wanted a document. This module makes agents hand you a proper deliverable — a weekly review, a research summary, a quote — in your brand and the same shape every single time. You'll build a Template in the Template Studio (Deliverables → Templates) with variables the agent fills, ask an agent to generate a branded PDF, Word or Excel deliverable from it via the generate_document tool, find it on the Deliverables page, and grade the reports your agents submit, 1–5 stars, on their Agent Details → Reports tab. The judgment underneath: a Template is the shape you author once so output stops drifting; the grade is the feedback loop that makes the next one better.
overview: This is the practitioner sibling of the 'agents should hand you a document, not just a chat reply' idea. If you came from AI Business Foundations, this is the machinery behind a playbook or mission that ends by producing something you can actually send — the deliverable is what that automation hands back. A Template defines the structure, sections, and formatting for a type of document, so an agent's reports, summaries, and analyses come out consistent every time instead of a different shape on every run. Templates live in the Template Studio (Deliverables → Templates). You set your Brand Kit once (logo and colours, under Deliverables → Brand kit); New template then offers a complete starting layout per category (the studio seeds starters such as Basic Report, Invoice, Executive Summary, Meeting Notes and Data Export), you edit its blocks, and variable chips fill in at generation time — {{user.name}} and {{date.long}} fill themselves, {{brand.*}} and {{company.*}} come from your brand kit and business profile, and data.* chips are the fields an agent (or you) supplies per document. The distinction that runs through the whole module is Template (the shape) versus Deliverable (the document the agent actually produces). Agents build the deliverable with the generate_document tool — a real platform tool the chatbot runs like any other — which renders a PDF, Word (DOCX) or Excel (XLSX) file in your brand and saves it to Deliverables with a link; from Chat you can just ask, 'Write a security audit report for the auth module using the Security Audit template.' On hosted Studio, branded documents and templates come with every plan. Keep one line straight: the file-type list in the Documents area (DOCX, XLSX, PPTX, PDF, MD, and more) describes what you can UPLOAD into a knowledge base; what agents generate is decided by their tools, not by that list. Separately, agents submit reports — after a task, after a scheduled routine, or when they find something noteworthy — and those live on each agent's Agent Details → Reports tab: each row shows a status, the title, when it arrived and its grade; open one in the viewer to read it and grade it 1–5 stars with an optional note, and the tab keeps the agent's average grade and its count of ungraded reports. Put it together and you have a loop a serious builder lives in: author a template so output stops drifting, generate against it, review and grade what agents hand back, then iterate the template until the shape is exactly right.
objectives: Explain what a Template is (the structure, sections, and formatting for a type of document) and why templating exists — so an agent's reports, summaries, and analyses come out consistent every time rather than a different shape on every run.

Create a Template in the Template Studio (Deliverables → Templates) — set the Brand Kit once, start New template from a layout, edit its blocks, place variable chips ({{user.name}}, {{date.long}}, {{brand.*}}, and the data.* fields an agent supplies per document), and Save template.

Distinguish a Template (the reusable shape) from a Deliverable (the document an agent produces via the generate_document tool — a branded PDF, DOCX or XLSX saved to Deliverables), and request a specific template from Chat (for example 'Write a security audit report for the auth module using the Security Audit template').

Find what agents produce: generated documents on the Deliverables page (the agent's reply links to each one), and agent reports on Agent Details → Reports — each row with its status, title, time and grade, opening into a viewer with the report's content, attachments and the agent that wrote it.

Grade a report 1–5 stars (optionally with a note) and explain how grades build a quality signal per agent — the Reports tab keeps each agent's average grade and its ungraded count — the feedback loop that improves future output.

Apply the format judgment: branded PDF, DOCX and XLSX generation through generate_document ships (on hosted Studio, with every plan), while the Documents file-type list describes what you can UPLOAD — what agents generate is decided by their tools, never by an upload list.

lessons.title: Templates — the shape you author once so output stops drifting
lessons.objective: Understand what a template is, why templating beats re-asking, and how to author one in the Template Studio from a layout of blocks plus variables.
lessons.body:
## The problem templates solve

Ask an agent for a report five times and you'll often get five different shapes: one has a summary at the top, one buries it at the bottom, one forgets the recommendations entirely. That's fine for a throwaway question and useless for anything you file, compare week-to-week, or hand to a colleague. A **Template** fixes it. A template **defines the structure, sections, and formatting for a type of document**, so when an agent needs to create a report, summary, or analysis, it *follows the template* — and the output comes out consistent every time.

Think of it as the difference between asking a new hire to "write up the security review" versus handing them a form with the sections already laid out. The form doesn't write the content — the reviewer still does the thinking — but it guarantees the *shape*. That's exactly what a template is: the shape, authored once, reused forever.

> **Vocabulary, fixed early.** The file an agent produces is a **Deliverable** — not an "output", "artifact", or "workspace file" in the words you use out loud. The reusable shape it's built from is a **Template**. Keep those two straight and the rest of this module is easy: *template = the shape, deliverable = the document*. Lesson 2 is entirely about that distinction.

## The starter templates

You don't start from a blank page. The Template Studio (**Deliverables → Templates**) seeds a set of starters in every workspace, one per common document type — for example:

| Starter | Format |
| --- | --- |
| **Basic Report** | PDF |
| **Invoice** | PDF |
| **Executive Summary** | PDF |
| **Meeting Notes** | Word (DOCX) |
| **Data Export** | Excel (XLSX) |

Notice what they have in common: each is a *recurring type of document* where consistency matters. An invoice that sometimes forgets the due date is a bad invoice; a report that changes shape every week is hard to skim. The docs suggest more you'd author yourself — a Daily Standup, a Security Audit, a Code Review, a Research Summary. The starters aren't a fixed menu you're limited to — they're examples of the pattern, and you'll author your own the same way.

## What a template is made of

A template is two things layered together:

1. **A layout of blocks.** Headings, text, tables, lists — the sections of the document, laid out as blocks you edit in the studio. This is the skeleton: *Summary*, *Findings*, *Actions*, *Recommendations*, or whatever suits the document type.
2. **Variables.** Chips written in double braces that are **filled in at generation time**. Some fill themselves — `{{user.name}}` and `{{date.long}}`, and `{{brand.*}}` and `{{company.*}}` from your brand kit and business profile. The `data.*` chips are the fields an agent (or you) supplies for each document: `{{data.target}}`, say, for what a security audit covers. Variables are what let one template serve many concrete documents: the same Security Audit template, filled with a different target and date each time it runs.

That second part is the crux. Without variables a template is just a static document. *With* them, it's a reusable form: the fixed parts (section headings, table columns, boilerplate) stay put, and the variable parts get filled at the moment of generation. Design a good template and you're really designing that split — what's fixed structure versus what's a fill-in-the-blank.

## Creating one: the studio's three steps

The Template Studio's own guide is short:

1. **Set your Brand Kit once** (**Deliverables → Brand kit**): upload your logo and pick your colours. Every document rendered from any template picks them up.
2. **Start from a layout, then edit.** Click **New template**, choose **Start from a layout** (a complete layout per category — letterhead for a letter, line items for an invoice) or **Blank**, name it, and edit the blocks and variable chips. Click **Save template**.
3. **Use it** from chat, a schedule, or a playbook — Lesson 2.

Like a playbook, the craft isn't in the clicking — it's in the blocks and the variables. A template whose sections are clear and whose `data.*` fields capture exactly the things that change run-to-run is a good template; a beautifully-named one with no structure is just an empty title.

## Worked walkthrough: reading a Security Audit template as a design

Take a **Security Audit** template you might author and read it as an anatomy exercise before you build your own. Its *purpose* is a structured security review with severity ratings, so a sensible structure has: a top **Summary** (one paragraph — what was reviewed, headline verdict), a **Findings** section (ideally a table with columns like *Issue*, *Severity*, *Location*, *Recommendation* — because a table forces every finding to carry a severity, which is the whole point of *this* document type), and a **Recommendations** section (prioritised next steps).

Now the variables. What changes every time this audit runs? The **module or system reviewed** and the **date**. So the template's header might read: *"Security Audit — {{data.target}} · {{date.long}}"*. Every time an agent generates against this template, `{{data.target}}` and `{{date.long}}` are filled with the real values, while the *sections and the severity-table columns stay identical*. That is a template doing its job: the auth-module audit this week and the billing-service audit next week come out as recognisably the same document, because you fixed the shape and let only the specifics vary.

Contrast that with *not* templating — just asking "do a security review of the auth module" cold each time. You'd get a security review, but its shape would drift, and comparing this week's to last week's would mean squinting past formatting differences. The template is what makes a *type* of document reproducible.

## Why this matters to a builder

Templating is the difference between an agent that answers and an agent that *delivers*. The moment you want output you'll file, compare, or send — anything beyond a one-off glance — you want it templated, because consistency is what makes a document trustworthy and skimmable. You've now got the shape. Next you'll turn it into an actual file.

knowledgeCheck.stem: What does a Template define, and what is the point of defining it?

options.text: The structure, sections, and formatting for a type of document — so an agent's reports, summaries, and analyses come out consistent every time
The model, temperature, and token budget an agent uses when it writes
The list of tools an agent is allowed to call while producing the document
The cron schedule on which a report is automatically generated

knowledgeCheck.explanation: A template defines the structure, sections, and formatting for a type of document, and the point is consistency — the agent follows the template so output doesn't drift shape run-to-run. Option b describes settings of an LLM call, not the document's shape. Option c describes tool scoping (a module 03 concern), not what a template is. Option d confuses a template (the shape) with a schedule (when something runs) — templates have nothing to do with cron timing.

knowledgeCheck.stem: In a template, what is a variable such as {{date.long}} or {{data.target}} for?

options.text: It marks a spot in the fixed structure that gets filled in automatically at generation time, so one template can serve many concrete documents
It is a comment that reminds the author what to write there but never appears in the output
It permanently hard-codes a value into every document, so it can never change between runs
It selects which agent is allowed to open the template

knowledgeCheck.explanation: Variables are the fill-in-the-blank chips — filled automatically at generation time — that let the same template produce many documents with the specifics (date, agent, target) varying while the structure stays fixed. Option b is wrong: a placeholder is replaced with a real value in the output, it isn't a hidden note. Option c is backwards — placeholders exist precisely so those values *do* vary each run; the structure is what stays fixed. Option d confuses a placeholder with a permission control, which it is not.

knowledgeCheck.stem: You're authoring a Security Audit template so every audit comes out the same shape. Which choice best reflects the fixed-structure vs fill-in-the-blank split?

options.text: Keep the section headings and a Findings table with a Severity column as fixed structure; make the reviewed target, the date, and the producing agent placeholders
Make every heading a placeholder so the sections change on each run, and hard-code one specific module name into the body
Put no structure in the template at all and rely on the agent to invent a fresh layout each time
Store the whole audit as a single placeholder called {{report}} that the agent fills with everything

knowledgeCheck.explanation: The point of templating a security audit is that the sections and the severity table stay identical while only the specifics vary — so headings and the Findings/Severity table are fixed, and target/date/agent are placeholders. Option b inverts it: making headings placeholders lets the shape drift (the exact failure templating prevents), and hard-coding one module name defeats reuse. Option c is 'no template' — it reintroduces the shape-drift problem. Option d collapses the whole document into one blank, which provides no structure and no consistency at all.

lessons.title: Template vs deliverable — generate_document and requesting a template from chat
lessons.objective: Separate the template (shape) from the deliverable (document) cleanly, know how an agent produces one via generate_document, and request a specific template from chat — while keeping the format lines straight.
lessons.body:
## Two words, one clean distinction

The single idea that makes this module click: **a Template is the shape; a Deliverable is the document an agent actually produces from it.** The template is reusable and lives in the Template Studio (Deliverables → Templates). The deliverable is a specific file, produced on a specific run, with the variables filled — this week's auth-module audit, tomorrow's billing-service audit. One template, many deliverables.

Agents build the deliverable with a real platform tool: **`generate_document`**. It sits in the agent's toolbox alongside the other tools it can call (the same lane as, for example, the meta-tool that runs connected-app actions). When an agent decides a task needs a produced document rather than a chat reply, it calls `generate_document` and hands back a deliverable. You don't invoke the tool by name yourself — you ask for the outcome ("write me the report") and the agent reaches for the tool. Frame it exactly as: **template = the shape, `generate_document` = produces the file.**

What it produces is a real file: a **PDF** (the default), a **Word (DOCX)** or an **Excel (XLSX)** document, laid out by your template and branded from your workspace's Brand Kit — saved to **Deliverables**, with a link in the agent's reply. (It can also render a social image or short video from one of your social templates.)

## How agents get to a template

Templates are **automatically available to agents** — you don't attach them per-agent. There are two ways a template gets used:

1. **A task or playbook calls for a format.** When a playbook step or a task specifies a particular output shape, the agent **references the matching template** on its own. This is how a nightly playbook can reliably end with a properly-structured standup or audit — the format is expected, so the agent uses the template for it.
2. **You ask in Chat.** You can request a template directly, in plain language:

> "Write a security audit report for the auth module using the Security Audit template"

The agent finds the named template, reads which `data.*` fields it needs, fills them from its work, generates a deliverable that follows the template's structure, and hands it back — a branded file saved to Deliverables. Naming the template in the request is how you steer the *shape* of what you get — same as picking the right form for the job.

> **ABF seam.** If you came from AI Business Foundations, this is the machinery behind "an agent should hand you a document." A playbook (ABF module 4) or a mission (ABF module 5) that ends by producing a deliverable is doing exactly this — its final step generates a templated document via `generate_document`, which is why the thing you get back has a consistent shape instead of being a loose chat message.

## The format lines — say exactly what ships

Here is where a careful practitioner earns trust, because it's easy to blur two lists. Three lines to keep straight:

- **Branded documents ship.** `generate_document` renders PDF, DOCX and XLSX, laid out by your template and branded from your workspace's Brand Kit (logo, colours, fonts). On hosted Studio, branded documents and templates come with every plan.
- **The template decides the shape; the format decides the file.** Meeting Notes is a Word layout and Data Export is a spreadsheet; pick (or build) the template that fits the job rather than converting afterwards.
- **The Documents file-type list is about UPLOADS, not generation.** The Documents area lists supported types — `.md`, `.txt`, `.csv`, `.json`, `.docx`, `.xlsx`, `.pptx`, `.pdf` (with OCR), code, `.html`. That list describes what the platform can **ingest into a knowledge base**. What an agent can *generate* is a separate question, answered by its tools — read "supported" in that list as "can be uploaded", never as "agents generate it".

Why be this fussy? Because the fastest way to lose a serious user is to promise an output because you saw its extension in an upload list. Ground your claims in the tool: `generate_document` makes branded PDF, DOCX and XLSX; for anything else, check what the agent's tools actually produce before you promise it.

## Worked walkthrough: one template, two deliverables

You've built the Security Audit template from Lesson 1. In Chat you ask: *"Write a security audit report for the auth module using the Security Audit template."* The agent finds the template, calls `generate_document`, fills `{{data.target}}` with "auth module" and `{{date.long}}` with today, and hands back **deliverable #1** — a branded PDF with your fixed sections and severity table, saved to Deliverables. Next week you ask the same thing for the billing service: same template, same `generate_document`, **deliverable #2** — identical shape, different specifics. One shape, two documents: that's the template/deliverable split in action.

And when a colleague asks "can it hand me that as a branded PDF for the client?", the answer is yes — that is what `generate_document` makes, in your brand kit. If they want Word or Excel, use a template in that format. If they want a format the tool doesn't make, say so rather than promising it. That's the difference between a builder who over-promises and one who's trusted: you claim what the tool makes, and you check anything else before you say it out loud.

knowledgeCheck.stem: What is the precise difference between a Template and a Deliverable?

options.text: A Template is the reusable shape; a Deliverable is the specific document an agent produces from it (via generate_document) with the placeholders filled
A Template is the finished file you send; a Deliverable is a draft that never leaves the workspace
They are the same thing under two names, used interchangeably
A Template is produced per run; a Deliverable is authored once and reused forever

knowledgeCheck.explanation: The template is the reusable shape you author once; the deliverable is the concrete document generated from it on a given run, placeholders filled — 'template = the shape, generate_document = produces the file.' Option b inverts which one is finished/sent — the deliverable is the produced document. Option c is wrong: they are deliberately distinct concepts, which is the whole point of the lesson. Option d swaps their roles — the deliverable is the per-run artifact and the template is the reusable one, not the reverse.

knowledgeCheck.stem: You want an agent to produce a report in a specific shape from Chat. What actually happens when you ask 'Write a security audit report for the auth module using the Security Audit template'?

options.text: Templates are automatically available to agents; the agent references the named template, calls generate_document to produce a deliverable that follows its structure, and fills the placeholders
You must first manually attach the template to that specific agent before it can see it
The agent pastes the raw template text back to you unfilled and asks you to complete it
Nothing — templates can only be used by scheduled playbooks, never from Chat

knowledgeCheck.explanation: Templates are automatically available to agents, and requesting one by name in chat is a documented path: the agent references the matching template, generates a deliverable via generate_document, and fills the placeholders. Option b is wrong — you don't attach templates per-agent; they're auto-available. Option c misdescribes the outcome: the agent produces a filled deliverable, it doesn't hand back the blank template. Option d is false — chat requests and playbook/task references are both documented ways to use a template.

knowledgeCheck.stem: A teammate points at the Documents area's list of supported file types and says 'so that's the list of formats our agents can generate.' What's the accurate correction?

options.text: That list is what you can UPLOAD into a knowledge base; what agents generate is set by their tools — generate_document makes branded PDF, DOCX and XLSX
It's correct — any format the platform can upload it can also generate, they're always the same set
It's the reverse: the list is generation formats, and nothing on it can be uploaded
The supported-types list refers to templates, so it dictates which template formats you may author

knowledgeCheck.explanation: The Documents supported-types list is about ingestion (what you can upload into a knowledge base); generation is a separate question, answered by the tools — generate_document renders PDF, DOCX and XLSX, branded from your workspace's Brand Kit, and saves them to Deliverables. Option b states the exact fallacy — upload support and generation output are separate lists. Option c inverts it: the list is precisely the uploadable types. Option d misattributes the list to templates; templates are built in the Template Studio, not governed by the upload list.

lessons.title: Where the work lands — Deliverables, agent reports, grading, and the feedback loop
lessons.objective: Find a generated document on the Deliverables page and an agent's reports on Agent Details → Reports, read a report in the viewer, grade it 1–5 stars, and understand how grades build a quality signal per agent — plus where reports are stored.
lessons.body:
## Two places your agents' work lands

Once an agent produces something, where does it go? Two places, and it pays to keep them apart:

- **Deliverables** — the files agents generate. Everything `generate_document` makes is saved to the **Deliverables** page (its Outputs view groups work into rows such as Reports, Documents and Spreadsheets), and the agent's reply links straight to the file it just made.
- **Agent reports** — what an agent *submits* about its own work: after completing a task, after a scheduled routine, or when it finds something noteworthy. They live on that agent's **Agent Details → Reports** tab, the running record of what it has done.

Reports arrive two ways:

- **Automatically** — when an agent finishes a scheduled routine or task, it submits a report summarising what it found, what it did, and anything needing attention. This is how a nightly playbook's work shows up without you asking.
- **On request** — you ask for one in Chat: *"Write a report on today's security findings."*

## Reading the Reports tab

Open an agent from the roster and go to its **Reports** tab. Each report is a row you can triage at a glance:

- **Status** — a coloured dot: ok, warning, critical, or info
- **Title** — what the report is about
- **Time** — when it was submitted
- **Grade** — its star rating, or a dash if you haven't graded it yet

Above the list the tab sums the agent up: how many reports, how many are OK and how many need attention, the **average grade**, and how many are still **ungraded**. That ungraded count is quietly useful: it's how you tell, across many reports, which ones are still waiting for a look.

## The viewer

Click a report and it opens in the **viewer**. It shows:

1. **The report itself** — its type and date, the title, the agent that wrote it, any metrics it carries, and the full content, rendered with its formatting and tables intact.
2. **Attachments** — files the report carries.
3. **The grade form** — plus a download of the content as a markdown file.

A typical report's *content* follows a recognisable shape — **Summary** (one-paragraph overview), **Findings** (the detailed results or observations), **Actions taken** (what the agent did — tool calls, changes), **Recommendations** (suggested next steps), and **Linked artifacts**. If that list feels familiar, it should: it's the same section thinking you put into a template in Lesson 1. A good template and a good report are the same shape seen from two ends.

## Grading — the feedback loop that matters

This is the part a serious builder cares about most. Every report can be **graded for quality** with a star rating:

1. Open the report in the viewer.
2. Select a **star rating (1–5)**.
3. Optionally add a **note**.
4. Submit the grade.

Grading isn't busywork — it's a **feedback loop**. The grade is saved on the report, and the agent's Reports tab keeps its **average grade** as grades accumulate. So a low grade isn't just a personal note; it's a signal in that agent's quality trend. Grade honestly and consistently and you build a real picture of which agents produce reliable work and which need their prompt, tools, or template tightened. Skip grading and you're flying blind — the average has nothing to work with.

That closes the loop this whole module has been building: author a template so output has a consistent shape (Lesson 1), generate a deliverable against it (Lesson 2), then **review and grade what your agents hand back** — and use what the grades tell you to iterate the template until the shape, and the quality, are exactly what you want.

## Where reports are stored

Reports aren't ephemeral chat scrollback — they're persisted records. The docs describe **two stores**:

- **The workspace filesystem**, at the path `/reports/{agent}/{date}_{slug}.md` — markdown, on disk under a per-agent folder.
- **The database**, for querying.

In the product, the agent's Reports tab keeps them, and the viewer downloads a report's content as a markdown file. That durable storage is why a report is a real artifact you can come back to, link to, and analyse — not a message that scrolls away. The `{agent}` folder and `{date}_{slug}` naming also means reports are organised by who produced them and when, which is the same axis you triage and grade along.

## Worked walkthrough: generate, find, read, grade

Follow one piece of work end to end. You ask in Chat for the auth-module security audit (Lesson 2); the agent generates it via `generate_document`, and its reply links to the new PDF on the **Deliverables** page. You open it and decide the findings are solid but the recommendations are thin, so you tighten the template's Recommendations section. That night the same agent finishes its scheduled review and submits a report; on its **Agent Details → Reports** tab there's a fresh row — a status dot, the title, a few minutes ago, no grade yet. You **open it** in the viewer, read it, and **grade it 3 stars with a note** ("good findings, weak recommendations"). The tab's ungraded count drops by one and the agent's average grade moves — a running signal of this agent's quality. Generated, found, read, graded — the full loop.

knowledgeCheck.stem: On an agent's Reports tab (Agent Details → Reports), what does each report's row show before you open it?

options.text: A status dot, the title, when it arrived, and its grade (a dash if ungraded)
The full rendered content of the entire report inline in the list
Only the agent's name, with no title, time, or status
The agent's system prompt and its complete tool configuration

knowledgeCheck.explanation: A row is a triage summary: a status dot, the title, when it arrived, and its grade (a dash until you grade it). Option b describes the viewer, which renders the full report when you open it, not the row. Option c understates the row, which carries several fields. Option d is unrelated — rows summarise a submitted report, they don't expose the agent's prompt or tool setup.

knowledgeCheck.stem: You grade a report 3 stars and add a comment. Beyond your own note, what does that grade actually do?

options.text: It's saved on the report and moves the agent's average grade on its Reports tab — a running quality signal on that agent's output
It deletes the report if the rating is below a threshold
It changes the model the agent will use on its next run
It is stored only on that one report and never counts towards anything

knowledgeCheck.explanation: The 1–5 star grade is saved on the report and counts towards the agent's average grade on its Reports tab, which is what makes grading a feedback loop rather than a private note. Option b invents a destructive behaviour — grading doesn't delete reports. Option c overstates it — a grade doesn't automatically switch models; it's a quality signal you act on. Option d contradicts how the tab works: every grade counts towards the agent's average.

knowledgeCheck.stem: Per the docs, where are agent reports persisted, and in what format on disk?

options.text: In the workspace filesystem at /reports/{agent}/{date}_{slug}.md (markdown) and in the database for querying
Only in the chat scrollback, so they disappear once the session ends
As branded PDF files in a shared cloud drive, with no database record
Only in the database as binary blobs, with nothing on the filesystem

knowledgeCheck.explanation: The docs put reports in the workspace filesystem at /reports/{agent}/{date}_{slug}.md — markdown on disk — and in the database for querying. Option b is wrong: reports are persisted artifacts, not ephemeral chat. Option c invents cloud-drive storage and drops the database record — neither matches the docs (branded PDFs are what generate_document makes for deliverables, a different thing from reports). Option d is half-right at best; storage is dual (filesystem + database), and the filesystem copy is markdown, not an opaque blob.

questions.explanation: In the Template Studio (Deliverables → Templates) you click New template, start from a layout (or Blank), edit the blocks and variable chips, and click Save template — with your Brand Kit set once beforehand. Option b invents a 'Save as Template' path from a chat message. Option c is the tool-connection flow from a different module, not template creation. Option d is an upload/convert/publish sequence unrelated to authoring a template.

questions.stem: When does a variable like {{date.long}} get its real value?

options.text: At generation time — it's filled in automatically when the agent produces the deliverable
When the template is first saved — the value is baked in permanently
Never — placeholders are decorative and appear as literal braces in the output
Only if a human manually edits every deliverable after it's produced

questions.explanation: Variables are filled automatically at generation time, which is what lets one template serve many deliverables with the specifics varying each run. Option b is wrong — baking the value in at save time would defeat the purpose; the value is resolved per generation. Option c contradicts the docs: variables are replaced with real values, not left as literal braces. Option d describes manual post-editing, whereas the fill is automatic at generation.

questions.stem: What tool do agents use to produce the actual deliverable document?

options.text: generate_document
composio_execute
workspace_write_file
platform_create_template

questions.explanation: generate_document is the platform tool an agent calls to produce a deliverable — 'template = the shape, generate_document = produces the file.' Option b, composio_execute, is the meta-tool for running connected-app actions, not document generation. Option c, workspace_write_file, writes raw files to the workspace but isn't the documented deliverable-generation tool. Option d isn't the generation tool — creating a template is authoring the shape, not producing a deliverable.

questions.stem: You ask in Chat: 'Write a security audit report for the auth module using the Security Audit template.' What makes this work without any per-agent setup?

options.text: Templates are automatically available to agents, so the agent references the named template and generates a deliverable that follows its structure
You must attach the Security Audit template to the agent's profile first
The Universal Router rewrites your message into a cron schedule
The agent can only use a template if it authored that template itself

questions.explanation: Templates are automatically available to agents, so naming one in a chat request is enough — the agent references it and generates a matching deliverable. Option b is wrong: no per-agent attachment is needed. Option c is irrelevant — routing your message to an agent has nothing to do with turning it into a schedule. Option d invents an authorship restriction that doesn't exist; any agent can use any available template.

questions.stem: A colleague sees '.docx', '.xlsx', and '.pdf' listed under supported file types in the Documents area and says 'so our agents generate Word, Excel, and PDF deliverables.' What's the accurate correction?

options.text: Right result, wrong reason: that list is what you can UPLOAD; generate_document is what makes branded PDF, DOCX and XLSX deliverables
They're right — the upload list and the generation list are always identical
They're wrong because those formats can't be uploaded either; only markdown can be uploaded
The list defines which templates you may author, so it does control generated formats

questions.explanation: The supported-types list describes ingestion (uploads into a knowledge base); generation comes from the tools, and generate_document does make Word, Excel and PDF deliverables, branded from the Brand Kit. The colleague lands on the right formats for the wrong reason — the same reasoning would wrongly promise every other uploadable type. Option b asserts the exact fallacy — the upload list and the generation list are separate. Option c is false: those office/PDF formats are uploadable (the list says so). Option d misreads the list as governing template authoring or generated formats, which it does not.

questions.stem: Which statement about generated deliverable formats is the accurate one to make today?

options.text: generate_document renders a PDF, DOCX or XLSX from your template, branded from the Brand Kit, and saves it to Deliverables
Branded output needs a paid add-on; without it every deliverable is plain text in the chat
Agents cannot produce documents at all; they can only reply in chat
Only PDF can be generated; Word and spreadsheet output are still on the roadmap

questions.explanation: generate_document is the shipped path: it renders PDF (the default), DOCX or XLSX laid out by your template, brands it from the workspace's Brand Kit, and saves it to Deliverables. Option b invents a paywall — on hosted Studio, branded documents and templates come with every plan. Option c under-claims — agents do produce documents via generate_document. Option d under-claims too: Word and Excel generation ship alongside PDF.

questions.stem: Where do agent-produced deliverables surface for you to review?

options.text: On the Deliverables page, linked from the agent's reply
The Marketplace → Playbooks tab
Settings → General
The Tools page, next to connected apps

questions.explanation: generate_document saves every document it makes to Deliverables, and the agent's reply links to it; reports an agent submits about its work sit on its Agent Details → Reports tab. Option b is where you install pre-built playbooks. Option c holds configuration, not produced deliverables. Option d is where you connect and assign tools, unrelated to reviewing what agents made.

questions.stem: Which values does each row on an agent's Reports tab display to help you triage?

options.text: A status dot, the title, when it was submitted, and its star grade (or a dash if ungraded)
The full markdown body, the agent's prompt, and the token cost of the run
Only a star rating with no other information
The workspace's billing plan and seat count

questions.explanation: Each row carries a status dot, the title, when it arrived, and its grade — a scannable triage summary. Option b describes the viewer's content plus run analytics, not the row. Option c understates the row; the grade is one of several fields. Option d is billing information, which isn't on a report row.

questions.stem: What does the report viewer show when you open a report?

options.text: Its type, date, title and agent, any metrics, the full rendered content, attachments, and the grade form
A blank editor for writing a brand-new report from scratch
The agent's raw system prompt and nothing else
A list of every other workspace's reports

questions.explanation: The viewer shows the report itself — type, date, title, the agent that wrote it, any metrics and the full rendered content — plus its attachments and the 1–5 star grade form. Option b is wrong — the viewer displays a submitted report, it isn't an authoring surface. Option c is far too narrow and incorrect: the viewer shows the report, not the agent's prompt. Option d violates workspace isolation and isn't what the viewer does — it shows this report, in this workspace.

questions.stem: How do you grade a report, and why does it matter beyond your own record?

options.text: Open it in the viewer, pick 1–5 stars (optionally a note) and submit; it moves the agent's average grade on its Reports tab
Type a number into the chat box; it only affects that single chat session
Grading is disabled unless you're on a paid tier
You grade the template, not the report, and it changes the template's structure

questions.explanation: You open the report, choose 1–5 stars (note optional) and submit, and the grade counts towards the agent's average grade on its Reports tab — a quality signal over time. Option b misdescribes the mechanism and its reach — grading is a report action, not a chat-only number. Option c invents a paywall; the docs describe grading as a standard action. Option d confuses the object — you grade the submitted report, and it doesn't rewrite the template.

questions.stem: Per the docs, where are agent reports stored persistently?

options.text: In the workspace filesystem at /reports/{agent}/{date}_{slug}.md and in the database for querying
Nowhere — they live only in the Reports tab and vanish on refresh
Only in an external cloud bucket you must connect yourself
Inside each template file, appended to the bottom

questions.explanation: Reports persist in the workspace filesystem at /reports/{agent}/{date}_{slug}.md and in the database for querying — dual storage. Option b is wrong: reports are durable artifacts, not transient UI. Option c invents a required external bucket; storage is the workspace filesystem plus the database. Option d is nonsensical — reports aren't appended into template files; templates are the reusable shape, reports are separate produced artifacts.

questions.stem: A typical agent report's content is organised into which sections?

options.text: Summary, Findings, Actions taken, Recommendations, and Linked artifacts
Subject, To, Cc, Bcc, and Attachments
Minute, Hour, Day-of-month, Month, Day-of-week
Public key, JWT, SSE endpoint, and callback URL

questions.explanation: A typical report is structured as Summary, Findings, Actions taken, Recommendations, and Linked artifacts — the same section thinking that goes into a good template. Option b is the header of an email, not a report's sections. Option c lists cron fields, unrelated to report content. Option d lists widget/auth concepts from a different module, not report sections.

questions.stem: You want to defend the claim 'a Template is not the same as a Deliverable' to a teammate. Which explanation is precise and correct?

options.text: The Template is the reusable shape you author once (structure + variables); a Deliverable is a specific document an agent produces from it via generate_document, with the variables filled — one template yields many deliverables
The Template is produced fresh on every run; the Deliverable is the single reusable form you author once
The Template is a graded report in Analytics; the Deliverable is the star rating you give it
They differ only by file extension — a Template is .md and a Deliverable is .pdf, otherwise identical

questions.explanation: The template is the reusable shape (structure plus placeholders); the deliverable is the concrete, per-run document generated from it via generate_document, so one template produces many deliverables. Option b swaps the roles — the deliverable is the per-run artifact, the template is the reusable one. Option c invents unrelated definitions (a grade is a quality signal, not a deliverable). Option d reduces a conceptual distinction to a file extension, and misstates it too — a template can be a PDF, Word or spreadsheet layout, and so can the deliverable made from it.

questions.stem: You've watched an agent generate weekly reviews for a month. The findings are always solid but the 'Actions' section is consistently thin, and your grades on its weekly reports hover at 2–3 stars. What's the most leveraged fix, and why?

options.text: Iterate the template — strengthen the Actions section so it prompts for specifics — because the template is the shared shape every generation follows, and the grades are the signal telling you where the shape is weak
Stop grading, since 2–3 stars is dragging down the analytics unfairly
Delete every past report so the low grades no longer pull down the agent's average grade
Switch the whole task to a fully-branded PDF, which will make the Actions section fill itself in

questions.explanation: Consistent weakness in one section across many runs points at the shared shape — the template — and the grades are exactly the feedback loop that localised the problem, so improving the template's Actions section is the highest-leverage fix. Option b throws away the feedback loop that just diagnosed the issue. Option c hides the signal instead of fixing the cause and defeats the point of quality tracking. Option d confuses format with content — changing the output format does nothing to make the Actions section richer; the template is what drives that.

labs.title: Author a template, generate a branded deliverable, and grade an agent's report
labs.goal: Produce your signature artifact for this module: a real, saved Template plus a branded Deliverable generated from it, found on the Deliverables page — and a graded agent report on Agent Details → Reports. You come away with a reusable template, a generated document, and a graded report you can point to.
labs.steps:
## What you'll build

A **Weekly Review** template with variables, a branded deliverable generated from it, and a grade on one of your agent's reports. This is the module's 'Try it now' turned into a guided build. Every step maps to the product: the Template Studio (Deliverables → Templates), the `generate_document` deliverable tool, the Deliverables page, and the agent's Reports tab.

### Before you start

- **Sign in.** Your personal workspace is created automatically on first login and you're the Admin, so you can do every step solo.
- **(Optional) Have something to summarise.** If you've done module 03, you may have documents in a Knowledge Base the review can draw on. Not required — you can ask the agent to review a topic or a pasted note instead.

### Part A — Author the template

1. **Set your Brand Kit** under **Deliverables → Brand kit** if you haven't: upload a logo and pick your colours. Every template picks them up.
2. **Go to Deliverables → Templates and click New template.** Choose **Start from a layout** (a report layout fits) or **Blank**.
3. **Name it 'Weekly Review'** and give it a one-line description (e.g. 'A weekly summary of progress, findings, and next actions').
4. **Shape the blocks.** Keep it section-based — headings for **Summary**, **Findings**, and **Actions**. Use a table under Findings if you want each finding to carry a consistent set of columns (this is the same 'fix the shape' thinking from Lesson 1).
5. **Add variables** for the things that change every week: `{{date.long}}` fills itself, and a `data.*` field such as `{{data.period}}` is one the agent supplies. A header line like *'Weekly Review — {{data.period}} · {{date.long}}'* is a good pattern.
6. **Click Save template.** It's now available to every agent in the workspace — you do NOT attach it to a specific agent.

### Part B — Generate a deliverable from it

7. **Open Chat** and ask an agent to generate against your template, in plain language — for example: *"Write this week's review using the Weekly Review template, based on my uploaded documents"* (or *"...based on this note: [paste]."*). Naming the template is how you steer the shape.
8. **Let it generate.** The agent finds the Weekly Review template, fills its `data.*` fields, calls `generate_document`, and hands back a **deliverable**: a branded PDF that follows your structure, saved to Deliverables, with a link in its reply. Note the distinction you just watched happen: the *template* was the shape, the *deliverable* is the produced document.

### Part C — Find it, then grade a report

9. **Open the deliverable** from the link in the reply, or find it on the **Deliverables** page. Confirm your sections are present, the variables are filled with real values, your brand kit is applied, and (if you added one) the Findings table rendered.
10. **Open the agent's Reports tab** (Agent Management → the agent → **Reports**). Open a report in the viewer, read it, and **grade it 1–5 stars** (add a note if you like). Watch the tab's ungraded count drop and the average grade update — it's a real feedback signal, not a throwaway. (No reports yet? Ask the agent in Chat to write a report on this week's work, then come back.)
11. **Iterate the template.** Based on what the deliverable looked like, go back and tweak the Weekly Review template — tighten a section that came out thin, add a variable you wished you had — then regenerate. Repeat until the shape is exactly what you want. That loop (author → generate → grade → iterate) is the whole point of the module.

### A note on cost

Generating a deliverable runs an AI model, and models cost money per use. The realistic setup for an operator is bring-your-own-key — supply your provider key in Settings and pay the provider directly. This exercise is short and cheap; keep it in mind for heavier or scheduled generation, where cheaper-model routing is your biggest cost lever.
checklist: Signed in and working in your own personal workspace
Set the Brand Kit (logo and colours) under Deliverables → Brand kit
Created a template named 'Weekly Review' in Deliverables → Templates (New template, from a layout or Blank)
Shaped clear sections (e.g. Summary / Findings / Actions), optionally a Findings table
Added variables ({{date.long}} and at least one data.* field) where they belong, and clicked Save template
Asked an agent in Chat to generate a deliverable USING the Weekly Review template by name
Opened the generated deliverable and confirmed it followed the template's structure, with variables filled and the brand kit applied
Opened an agent's Reports tab and read a report in the viewer
Graded the report 1–5 stars (optionally with a note) and saw the ungraded count and average grade update
Iterated the template at least once and regenerated to improve the shape
ARTIFACT SAVED: your Weekly Review template, a generated deliverable and a graded report, kept as proof of the full loop

resources.title: Automatos AI — Templates (platform docs)
resources.annotation: The docs page for templates: what a template is (structure, sections, formatting for a type of document), example templates to author (Daily Standup, Security Audit, Code Review, Research Summary), and how templates are available to agents and requested from chat ('...using the Security Audit template'). Its create flow describes markdown templates (+ New Template → markdown structure → {{placeholder}} variables → Save); the product's Template Studio (Deliverables → Templates) builds PDF, Word and spreadsheet templates from blocks and variable chips, which is what Lesson 1 and the lab follow.

resources.title: Automatos AI — Reports (platform docs)
resources.annotation: The docs page for agent reports: report contents (Summary / Findings / Actions taken / Recommendations / Linked artifacts), a viewer, 1–5 star grading, and persistent storage at /reports/{agent}/{date}_{slug}.md plus the database. It places reports on an older Activity page, as cards; in the product they live on each agent's Agent Details → Reports tab (status, title, time, grade, average grade, ungraded count), and generated documents live on the Deliverables page.

resources.title: Automatos AI — Documents & supported file types (platform docs)
resources.annotation: Read this specifically for the supported file-types table (.md/.txt/.csv/.json, .docx/.xlsx/.pptx, .pdf with OCR, code, .html). The critical practitioner point: that list is what you can UPLOAD into a knowledge base; what agents generate is decided by their tools (generate_document makes branded PDF, DOCX and XLSX). Don't read an upload list as a generation promise.

resources.title: Automatos AI — Agent Analytics (platform docs)
resources.annotation: The docs page for agent analytics. The docs say report grades feed agent quality tracking here; in the product today a grade shows on the agent's own Reports tab (average grade, ungraded count). Either way it's the destination end of the feedback loop that makes grading worth doing — grade honestly and the signal becomes real.

resources.title: Automatos AI — the generate_document deliverable tool (orchestrator/consumers/chatbot/service.py)
resources.annotation: The real platform tool agents call to produce a deliverable: it renders a PDF (the default), DOCX or XLSX — or a social image or video from a social template — brands it from the workspace's Brand Kit, and saves it to Deliverables with a link. This is a code source (proves the tool exists and how it's wired), the grounding for 'template = the shape, generate_document = produces the file.'

resources.title: Automatos AI — Document Generation module (PRD-63, architecture direction)
resources.annotation: The WHY behind deliverables: deliverables are the 'last mile' that turns AI analysis into documents a business actually sends, and the design intent is templated output in PDF/DOCX/XLSX. That output now ships through generate_document and the Template Studio, branded from the Brand Kit; read the PRD for the reasoning behind it.

resources.title: Automatos AI — Missions (platform docs)
resources.annotation: Context for how a deliverable is the end of a bigger piece of work: a mission (an autonomous objective an agent plans and you approve) can conclude by generating a templated deliverable — the document saved to Deliverables, or the report on the agent's Reports tab, is often what a mission or a scheduled playbook hands back. Useful for connecting this module to earlier ones; the deliverable is the output, not the orchestration.
